name: Geji
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 7 other works consulted do not discuss stress; 1 further work by the same author (or citing it for stress) agrees.
catalog_citation: Caron, Bernard. 2008. Depressor consonants in Geji. Special World Congress of African Linguistics 6 (Special WOCAL 6: Exploring the African Language Connection in the Americas), São Paulo, 11-15 August 2008, pp. 129-138 [per HAL cover sheet]. Author's version, HAL halshs-00645129 (11 pp. incl. cover). Corroborated by Caron, Bernard. 2013. Tonal inversion in Geji and Pelu. In Henry Tourneux (ed.), Topics in Chadic Linguistics VII, 77-86. Cologne: Rüdiger Köppe; HAL preprint halshs-00647257v2.
catalog_locator: Caron 2008, paper p. 1 (p. 2 of the HAL file; p. 1 is the HAL cover sheet), opening paragraph. Corroboration: Caron 2013 HAL preprint p. 2, footnote 1.
catalog_quote: Geji has a tonal system based on a three-level distinction between Hi, Mid and Low, with Falling and Rising combinations of Hi and Lo. This system is fully operational in both grammar and lexicon, but it may be the result of the interaction between a set of voiced consonants called depressor consonants and a deeper two-level opposition between Hi and non-Hi tones. The effect of depressor consonants in Geji can best be observed in verbal nouns. [Caron 2008 p. 1] ... Geji and Pelu (resp. G. and P.) both have 3-tones. High tone (H) is noted by an acute accent on the vowel (á), Low tone (L) with a grave accent (à), and Mid tone (M) with a macron (ā). Falling tone (F) is noted by a circumflex accent (â), and Rising tone (R) by a caron (ǎ). [Caron 2013 preprint p. 2 fn. 1]
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: Geji has a tonal system based on a three-level distinction between Hi, Mid and Low, with Falling and Rising combinations of Hi and Lo. This system is fully operational in both grammar and lexicon, but it may be the result of the interaction between a set of voiced consonants called depressor consonants and a deeper two-level opposition between Hi and non-Hi tones. The effect of depressor consonants in Geji can best be observed in verbal nouns.
new_statements.citation: Caron, Bernard. 2008. Depressor consonants in Geji. Paper presented at Special WOCAL 6, São Paulo, 11-15 August 2008. HAL halshs-00645129.
new_statements.locator: p. 1, opening paragraph (PDF page 2 of the HAL file; the first page is the HAL cover sheet). Corroborated by Caron 2013, Tonal inversion in Geji and Pelu, HAL preprint p. 2 fn. 1: 'Geji and Pelu (resp. G. and P.) both have 3-tones.'
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (HAL halshs-00645129, 11 pp., text present). extracted text of PDF page 2 (paper p. 1, after the HAL cover sheet) gives the opening paragraph exactly as quoted: "Geji1 has a tonal system based on a three-level distinction between Hi, Mid and Low, with Falling and Rising combinations of Hi and Lo. This system is fully operational in both grammar and lexicon, but it may be the result of the interaction between a set of voiced consonants called depressor consonants and a deeper two-level opposition between Hi and non-Hi tones. The effect of depressor consonants in Geji can best be observed in verbal nouns." The only difference is the footnote superscript on "Geji1". The HAL cover sheet…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Geji is described as a lexical and grammatical tone language with three level tones (H, M, L) plus falling and rising contours; tone patterns are conditioned by depressor (voiced obstruent) initials and floating H tones. Neither Caron 2008 nor Caron 2013 mentions word stress, accent or prominence at all; no stress rule is stated and no claim of absence of stress is made explicitly.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tonal notes: verbal nouns take an all-L pattern after voiced-obstruent initials and all-M otherwise (Caron 2008 §1); Geji pre-pausal nouns cannot carry a rising pattern, unlike Pelu (Caron 2013 §1); H tones cannot link to syllables beginning with a depressor consonant (Caron 2013).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone in the lexicon and grammar (nouns, verbal nouns, noun + quantifier phrases); Caron 2013 additionally treats pre-pausal (citation/phrase-final) forms versus non-final forms. Data are from the Geji dialect (village of Geji), with Pelu compared in the 2013 paper.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog nucl1692 'Gyaazi' (ISO gyz) is the Geji dialect cluster with dialects Bolu [bolu1244], Geji [geji1247] and Pelu [pelu1234]. All of Caron's Geji data are from the Geji dialect (Geji village, east of Zaranda mountain, Bauchi State); Caron 2013 compares it with Pelu. Caron treats Zaranda (Buu) as a separate language of the Geji cluster (his 2008 Bu/Zaranda notes, held here, are NOT Gyaazi); Blench 2020 and Wikipedia instead group Buu, Gyaazi and Mәgang (Mugan) as three varieties of 'Geji'. The quoted statement therefore describes the Geji dialect proper.

new_statements.quote: Geji and Pelu (resp. G. and P.) both have 3-tones. High tone (H) is noted by an acute accent on the vowel (á), Low tone (L) with a grave accent (à), and Mid tone (M) with a macron (ā). Falling tone (F) is noted by a circumflex accent (â), and Rising tone (R) by a caron (ǎ).
new_statements.citation: Caron, Bernard. 2013. Tonal inversion in Geji and Pelu. In Henry Tourneux (ed.), Topics in Chadic Linguistics VII: Papers from the 6th Biennial International Colloquium on the Chadic Languages, Villejuif, September 22-23, 2011, 77-86. Cologne: Rüdiger Köppe.
new_statements.locator: Footnote 1, HAL preprint p. 2 (PDF page 3; page 1 is the HAL cover sheet). Whole paper read: 6 text pages, sections 1-5 plus abbreviations and references.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: 7 pages, text, no scanned needed). Footnote 1 on PDF page 3 (preprint p. 2, HAL cover sheet is page 1) reads exactly: 'Geji and Pelu (resp. G. and P.) both have 3-tones. High tone (H) is noted by an acute accent on the vowel (á), Low tone (L) with a grave accent (à), and Mid tone (M) with a macron (ā). Falling tone (F) is noted by a circumflex accent (â), and Rising tone (R) by a caron (ǎ).' — verbatim match. I re-read all six text pages (intro + Table 1 classification, sect. 1 pre-pausal tonal inversion with Table 3, sect. 2 stabilizer =kən and floating H, sect. 3 quantifier gwon, sect. 4 tone-combination rules and intonational downdrift, sect. 5 conclusion, abbreviations, references). It…
new_statements.relation_note: Same picture as the existing statement from Caron 2008 (three-level tone system H/M/L with F and R contours; nothing about stress). Adds only that the Pelu dialect shares the three-tone system and that intonational downdrift shapes pre-pausal noun tones. The catalog record for Geji has an empty rule, and this work supplies none, so it confirms 'tone language, no stress statement' rather than filling the rule.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The paper treats Geji (and the Pelu dialect) as a three-level tone language (H, M, L, plus Falling and Rising contour tones) and works out tone-spreading, tone-copying, floating-H and downdrift rules for pre-pausal nouns, the stabilizer =kən and the quantifier gwòn. It never mentions word stress, prominence or accent in the sense of stress; 'accent' occurs only as the name of the diacritics (acute, grave, circumflex).
new_statements.exceptions: None about stress. Tonal detail only: Geji proper disallows rising melodies (R, MH) on pre-pausal nouns where Pelu has them (Table 3); rising melodies do occur in verbs (mə̄ pākí wī 'we finished'); pre-pausal LL forms are attributed to intonational downdrift (sect. 4-5).
new_statements.identity_note: Caron 2013 covers two dialects of the Geji language, Geji proper and Pelu; its Table 1 lists the Geji language with dialects Bolu, Pelu, Geji, matching Glottolog nucl1692's three dialects. Zaranda (Buu) and Dir are separate languages of the Geji cluster and are not the subject of the paper. The tonal-inversion facts (no rising melodies on pre-pausal nouns) are specific to Geji proper; Pelu keeps the rising melodies.
